method: Every driver call ran through a pymongo CommandListener; each step's 'wire' holds the exact aggregate/getMore/killCursors/insert/update/delete/drop/collMod commands and raw replies (lsid removed, $clusterTime signature hash omitted; empty getMores are summarised as a count with durations plus one full sample).

Events were read with stream.try_next() in a loop (max_await_time_ms=1000, 0.2 s pause after an empty batch) until the wanted count or the timeout (30 s unless the step says otherwise), plus a short extra wait to catch unexpected events.
Raw probes used db.command(aggregate/getMore/killCursors) inside one explicit session so the server's reply or error is recorded without driver retries.
Events seen on the cluster-level stream from databases other than mt_cs were only counted by namespace and operationType (none were seen).
Steps prefixed x, cr, er and fr go beyond the spec's (a)-(f) to explain or confirm what (a)-(f) showed; they touched only collections inside mt_cs.

conclusions.question: (a) Does collection.watch() work on a single-shard managed cluster with no feature enabled?
conclusions.answer: Yes. db.mt_cs.cs_a.watch() opened (aggregate {$changeStream: {}} returned a live cursor with a postBatchResumeToken and an operationTime) and delivered the insert, $set update and delete in the first getMore, 0.34 s after the writes, with no portal, CLI or collMod step. Writes issued right after watch() returned and before any getMore were captured, so the start point is fixed when the aggregate runs. Empty getMores block for maxTimeMS (about 1.08 s at 1000 ms, 3.08 s at 3000 ms) and always return a postBatchResumeToken.

conclusions.question: (a) What do change events look like?
conclusions.answer: Keys in this order: _id {_data: <base64 string>}, operationType, wallTime (BSON date, millisecond precision), fullDocument (insert and update only), documentKey {_id}, ns {db, coll}. There is no clusterTime, txnNumber, lsid or collectionUUID field. Delete events have no fullDocument. replace_one is reported as operationType 'update' with the new document in fullDocument; no 'replace' event was seen. _data base64-decodes to ASCII colon-separated integers such as '3:0:186840832:0:186840832:1:0'; the third and fifth fields grow by about 200-300 per small write (LSN-like), and with startAtOperationTime the seventh field holds the start time in microseconds since 2000-01-01.

conclusions.question: (a) Do update events carry updateDescription?
conclusions.answer: No. Not by default, not with updateLookup, and not after collMod {enableUpdateDescription: true}: the boolean form is accepted and listCollections shows enableUpdateDescription: true, but update events from $set+$unset, $inc, $push, a pipeline-style update and replace_one still had no updateDescription, also a minute later on a new client and stream. The Learn-documented form {enableUpdateDescription: {enabled: true}} is rejected with code 14 TypeMismatch ('The BSON field 'collMod.enableUpdateDescription' has an incorrect type 'object'; it should be one of the following valid types: [bool, long, int, decimal, double]'). Every update event carries fullDocument (the post-update document) even without updateLookup. Whether a cluster-level preview toggle turns updateDescription on was not tested, because this phase forbids cluster changes.

conclusions.question: (b) What does full_document='updateLookup' do?
conclusions.answer: It is accepted and the events look the same as without it: insert and update events carry fullDocument, delete events do not. The fullDocument of an update is the document as of that update, not a lookup at read time: two updates written before the read came back with qty 2 and qty 3, and an update followed by a delete still carried the post-update document (qty 4) instead of null.

conclusions.question: (c) Does a database-level stream (db.watch()) work?
conclusions.answer: It opens but never delivered an event. aggregate: 1 with $changeStream on mt_cs returns a cursor (ns mt_cs.$cmd.aggregate) whose getMores honour maxTimeMS and advance the postBatchResumeToken, but in five tests (inserts into two existing collections; insert, update and delete on a new collection; a side-by-side run where a collection stream got the same insert in 0.15 s; a raw aggregate with three getMores; a resume from a token that preceded ten mt_cs writes) it returned no events and no error (windows of 9 to 45 s). Agents should not rely on db.watch() on this service; use collection streams, or client.watch() with a $match on ns.db.

conclusions.question: (c) Does a cluster-level stream (client.watch()) work?
conclusions.answer: Yes. client.watch() sends aggregate: 1 on admin with {$changeStream: {allChangesForCluster: true}} and delivered the mt_cs insert 0.16 s after the write; a $match on ns.db in the pipeline is applied server-side and delivered the mt_cs event alone. A collection stream through the .global. host also works (insert delivered in 0.1 s).

conclusions.question: (d) Does resume_after replay the events missed while the stream was closed?
conclusions.answer: Yes. A token from the last event read, reused with resume_after after the stream was closed, returned exactly the three writes made while no stream was open (insert, update, delete) in order in the aggregate's firstBatch, with no duplicate of the token's own event; start_after behaved identically. stream.resume_token equals the last event _id after a batch; on an idle stream it is the postBatchResumeToken, which also resumed correctly, so an idle consumer can checkpoint.

conclusions.question: (e) What errors do malformed or fabricated resume tokens give?
conclusions.answer: All at the aggregate (PyMongo raises them from watch()), none with errorLabels: non-base64 _data gives code 2 BadValue 'Encoded Resume token is invalid'; empty _data, a MongoDB-style hex token, a truncated real token, a real token with one byte flipped, all-0x00 or all-0xFF bytes, version field 9, too few fields, a non-numeric field, or base64 of plain text give code 2 BadValue 'Resume token is invalid'; _data that is not a string, {} or {foo: 'bar'} give code 40647 ChangeStreamBadResumeToken 'Bad resume token: _data missing or of wrong type. Expected string, got { ... }'; resumeAfter given as a string gives code 14 TypeMismatch 'The BSON field 'resumeAfter' has an incorrect type 'string'; it should be of type 'object'.'; a position field of 1 or 10,000,000 gives code 72 InvalidOptions 'Expired resume token or cursor, reinitialize the change stream cursor'. Accepted without error: trailing bytes appended to a real token, a position one below a real event (that event was not replayed), and a position 100 times ahead, which then skipped a new insert for 15 s, so a corrupted future token yields a silently idle stream.

conclusions.question: What does the service return for a resume token that can no longer be resumed (DECISIONS change-streams open item 1)?
conclusions.answer: For a token whose position lies below the oldest change the service still holds: code 72 InvalidOptions 'Expired resume token or cursor, reinitialize the change stream cursor' at the aggregate, with no errorLabels; not 286 ChangeStreamHistoryLost, and 40647 ChangeStreamBadResumeToken appears only for a structurally bad token. This was produced with fabricated tokens (positions 1 and 10,000,000 failed; 100,000,000 and 170,000,000 were accepted) on a cluster about 40 minutes old whose whole change log fits in the active 400 MB, so a real token that rotated out of the 400 MB log or past the 35-day window was not exercised and may behave differently.

conclusions.question: (e) What happens with a token from a dropped and recreated collection, and when a watched collection or database is dropped?
conclusions.answer: No error anywhere. Dropping a watched collection emits no drop or invalidate event: the server kills the cursor and the next getMore fails with code 43 CursorNotFound 'Cursor not found in server' (no labels), which PyMongo treats as resumable and silently re-opens with resumeAfter, so the stream stays alive and later delivers inserts into the recreated collection. resume_after and start_after with a token taken before the drop open on the recreated collection and deliver its new inserts. dropDatabase behaves the same (no dropDatabase or invalidate event, CursorNotFound, one driver resume per stream). Tokens are not bound to a collection: a cs_d token is accepted on cs_e, and the same event carried different _id values in two streams, so an event _id is a stream position, not a stable event identity for de-duplication.

conclusions.question: (f) Does start_at_operation_time work, including old and future times?
conclusions.answer: Yes. A timestamp 3.5 minutes old replayed the three marker writes, as did hello's operationTime taken just before them, while a timestamp 210 s old on a collection whose only events were 13 minutes old returned nothing (control). Timestamps from before the cluster existed (1 hour ago) and 40 days ago were accepted with no error and replayed from the oldest retained change; a time 2 minutes in the future was accepted and skipped current writes. operationTime is wall-clock seconds, and its increment field appears to hold microseconds. Write replies carry no operationTime (session.operation_time stays None) and events carry no clusterTime, so a start time has to come from the operationTime of hello, aggregate or getMore, from event wallTime, or from the wall clock.

conclusions.question: Are pre-images (fullDocumentBeforeChange) available without a cluster feature?
conclusions.answer: Yes. collMod {changeStreamPreAndPostImages: {enabled: true}} is accepted and full_document_before_change='whenAvailable' returned the pre-update document on update and delete events. On a collection without it, 'required' opens but the first getMore after an update fails with code 10065 Location10065 'Change stream was configured to require a pre-image for all update, delete and replace events, but the pre-image was not found for event' (no labels).

conclusions.question: Is showExpandedEvents supported?
conclusions.answer: No: code 115 CommandNotSupported 'BSON field 'showExpandedEvents' is not supported' at open. This matches the Learn change-streams limitation and contradicts the $changeStream operator page that lists the parameter without a caveat.

conclusions.question: Do server-side pipelines and streams on not-yet-existing collections work?
conclusions.answer: Yes. [{$match: {operationType: {$in: ['insert', 'delete']}}}, {$project: {fullDocument: 0}}] dropped the update event and removed fullDocument from the insert; watch() on a collection that did not exist yet opened and delivered the insert that created it.

collection_level_changes_inside_mt_cs: All removed with dropDatabase mt_cs in z1.
cleanup: All change streams were closed (killCursors replies list every cursor as killed) and database mt_cs was dropped; list_database_names() no longer contains mt_cs.
